facts.statement: Panderichthys was a lobe-finned fish that lived during the Late Devonian period, approximately 380 million years ago.
facts.quote: Panderichthys is a genus of extinct sarcopterygian (lobe-finned fish) from the late Devonian period, about 380 Mya.

facts.statement: Fossils of Panderichthys were recovered from Frasnian deposits in Latvia.
facts.quote: Panderichthys, which was recovered from Frasnian (early Late Devonian) deposits in Latvia, is represented by two species.

facts.statement: The genus Panderichthys is named after the paleontologist Christian Heinrich Pander.
facts.quote: It is named after the German-Baltic paleontologist Christian Heinrich Pander.

facts.statement: The species Panderichthys rhombolepis was discovered by Gross in 1930, while Panderichthys stolbovi was discovered and illustrated by Emilia Vorobyeva in 1960.
facts.quote: P. rhombolepis was discovered by Gross in 1930 and P. stobolvi was discovered and figured by Emilia Vorobyeva in 1960.

facts.statement: The type species Panderichthys rhombolepis was found in Lode, Latvia.
facts.quote: P. rhombolepis was discovered in Lode, Latvia within Frasnian deposits

facts.statement: Shultze and Arsenault were the first researchers in 1985 to recognize that Panderichthys was phylogenetically closer to tetrapods than to fish.
facts.quote: The first time they were recognized as being phylogenetically closer to tetrapods than fish was by Shultze and Arsenault in 1985.

facts.statement: Panderichthys was a fish measuring between 1.5 and 2 meters in length with a large, flattened, tetrapod-like head.
facts.quote: Panderichthys is a 1.5-2 m long fish with a large tetrapod-like head that is flattened, narrow at the snout and wide in the back.

facts.statement: The vertebral column of Panderichthys was fully ossified and its vertebrae were comparable to those of early tetrapods.
facts.quote: The vertebral column is ossified throughout its length and the vertebrae are comparable to those of early tetrapods.

facts.statement: Panderichthys shares ten specific anatomical features with tetrapods, including a flat skull roof, paired frontals, no external intracranial joint, and complex polyplocodont teeth.
facts.quote: Panderichthys shares ten features with tetrapods: The skull roof is flat compared to fish skulls. The orbits are more dorsal and lie closer together. The external naris is close to the margin of the upper jaw. Frontals are paired. There is no external intracranial joint. The parietal bone is located between the orbits and main portion posterior to orbits. In P. rhombolepis, the squamosal touches the maxilla (varies among specimens though). The teeth have a complex polyplocodont structure. A lack of median fins. In panderichthyids and Ichthyostega, the ribs are attached to the neural arch and there is an intercentrum.

facts.statement: The humerus of Panderichthys exhibits a mix of both primitive and derived anatomical features.
facts.quote: The humerus of Panderichthys displays a variety of features including ones that are both primitive and derived.

facts.statement: Analysis of the humerus suggests that the evolutionary transition from fish-like limb structures to tetrapod limbs occurred more slowly than previously thought.
facts.quote: The result of the analysis of the humerus of Panderichthys is that the transition of the humerus from the fish-like organisms to tetrapods occurred much slower than previously thought

facts.statement: Panderichthys was likely able to prop up its large head, a capability that probably aided in breathing.
facts.quote: This resulted in the ability of Panderichthys to prop up its large head most likely to breathe.

facts.statement: The small, finger-like bones in Panderichthys lack muscle development and joints, representing an intermediate form between fish fins and tetrapod limbs.
facts.quote: These finger-like bones show neither muscle development nor joints and they are extremely small, but nonetheless show an intermediate form between fully fish-like fins and tetrapods.

facts.statement: The discovery of possible tetrapod tracks predating Panderichthys suggests that the genus was not a direct ancestor of tetrapods.
facts.quote: Possible tetrapod tracks dating back to before the appearance of Panderichthys in the fossil record were reported in 2010, which suggests that Panderichthys is not a direct ancestor of tetrapods

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Panderichthys is Panderichthys rhombolepis.
facts.quote: type_species: Panderichthys rhombolepis

facts.statement: The genus Panderichthys was described by Gross in 1941.
facts.quote: authority: Gross, 1941

facts.statement: The genus Panderichthys includes the species Panderichthys stolbovi (described by Vorobyeva in 1960) and Panderichthys rhombolepis (described by Gross in 1941).
facts.quote: subdivision: * P. stolbovi? Vorobyeva, 1960 P. rhombolepis Gross, 1941

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Panderichthys may have used its pectoral fins to anchor itself while moving forward via side-to-side body undulation.
facts.quote: Boisvert describes the locomotion of Panderichthys as possibly using one of its pectoral fins to anchor itself while side to side undulation propels the body forward.

facts.statement: Although Panderichthys has a tetrapod-like head shape, it retains an intracranial joint characteristic of fish.
facts.quote: From the outside, Panderichthys has a tetrapod-like head, but actually retains an intracranial joint that is a characteristic of fish.

facts.statement: The teeth of Panderichthys have a polyplocodont structure.
facts.quote: In addition, the teeth are of polyplocodont structure.

facts.statement: Panderichthys is considered at least a facultative air breather, representing an intermediate stage in the evolution of air breathing.
facts.quote: Sarcopterygians such as Panderichthys can be considered at least facultative air breathers and demonstrate an intermediate form as air breathing was becoming more abundant.

facts.statement: Recent studies redefine Elpistostegalia as a clade starting with Panderichthys and including all living tetrapods.
facts.quote: More recent studies tend to redefine Elpistostegalia in an expanded format, as a clade starting at Panderichthys and encompassing everything as far as living tetrapods (the tetrapod crown group).

facts.statement: Panderichthys lived during the late Devonian (Frasnian) period in Lode, Latvia.
facts.quote: Panderichthys was alive during the late Devonian (Frasnian) in Lode, Latvia.

facts.statement: Panderichthys is hypothesized to have been adapted for moving in shallow, debris-filled waters in a marginal marine environment.
facts.quote: Lode is known to be a marginal marine environment and it has been hypothesized that Panderichthys was adapted for movement in shallow and debris filled waters.

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that P. rhombolepis was a large predator feeding on dipterids, small and juvenile sarcopterygians, and Latvius.
facts.quote: Within this environment it has been hypothesized that P. rhombolepis was a large predator and fed upon dipterids, small and juvenile sarcopterygians, and Latvius.

facts.statement: Due to its size and co-occurrence with bite-marked heterostracans, Panderichthys may have been a major predator of these armored jawless fish.
facts.quote: Panderichthys is an outlier in size and bite mark co-occurrence compared to many other jawed vertebrates, so it may have been a major predator of heterostracans.

facts.statement: The species P. rhombolepis was described by Gross in 1941.
facts.quote: species_authority: Gross, 1941

facts.statement: Panderichthys was an extinct genus of lobe-finned fish similar to a tetrapod that lived during the Late Devonian (Frasnian) period, 380 million years ago.

facts.statement: Its most notable feature was a vertical spiracle opening above its head, used to draw water while buried in mud.

facts.statement: During evolution, this spiracle transformed into the stapes, one of the three bones of the middle ear.

facts.statement: The genus lived from the Givetian to the Frasnian stages, between 387.95 and 372.15 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Givetian to Frasnian (387.95 to 372.15 million years ago)

facts.statement: It is considered the closest evolutionary relative to tetrapods that still possessed fins.
facts.quote: Panderichthys se considera el pariente evolutivo más cercano a los tetrápodos que aún poseía aletas

facts.statement: It was the ancestor of the first tetrapods, from which all other land vertebrates, including humans, descended.
